Brand identity vs logo design: what are you actually buying?

A practical guide to the difference between a mark, an identity system and the strategy that makes either useful.

By VisionCraft Labs · 4 min read

Start with the problem, not the deliverable

A request for a new logo often begins with a broader problem: the business has changed, the website feels inconsistent or the sales presentation no longer explains the offer well. Before deciding what to commission, identify where the current identity is falling short.

If the only problem is a technically poor logo file, a focused asset repair may be enough. If every communication looks unrelated, the missing piece is more likely a system.

What a logo does

A logo is an identifying mark. It should reproduce clearly in the places the business needs it: a website header, proposal, product, invoice or small social profile. A logo project may include variations and files, but it does not automatically define the rest of the brand experience.

Ask which formats, color versions, minimum sizes and usage guidance are included. An attractive presentation is not a substitute for files your team can use.

What an identity system adds

An identity system defines how the brand behaves visually. Typography, color, image direction, spacing and composition work alongside the logo. Applications show how those rules translate into actual communication.

The useful test is whether someone can create a new page or presentation that belongs to the same brand without copying the original layout. A good system provides enough direction to make that possible.

Where strategy fits

Strategy clarifies the audience, offer and position that the identity needs to express. It gives design decisions a business context and helps the team judge ideas against something more useful than personal preference.

The depth of strategy should match the uncertainty. A well-defined business may need a concise alignment phase; a new or changing proposition may need more exploration.

How to write a better brief

Describe what has changed, who the brand needs to reach and where the identity must work. Share the current assets and the practical constraints. Be explicit about a protected logo or other elements that must remain.

Ask for a scope that separates strategic work, identity development, applications and handover. This makes proposals easier to compare and reduces ambiguity about what happens after approval.
